title: How often should you train for BODYBUILDING
summary: NH argues that weekly set counts are meaningless without frequency: when sets happen matters more than how many. He derives 2-4 sets per muscle per session at roughly 48-hour intervals, giving about 7-14 sets per week, explains that frequency should dictate the template, and introduces evolving set ranges for advanced lifters.
claims: Most YouTube advice on weekly sets per muscle (12 or 15) gives arbitrary numbers and ignores frequency entirely
Knowing when sets occur is as important as, or more important than, how many sets you do: the when comes before the how much
A coach who prescribes 12 weekly sets but says to do them whenever does not understand frequency and therefore programming
The same 9 weekly sets can be done as 9 in one day, 3x3 across three days, or 6+3, and each distribution gives a completely different result
Doing 9 sets for one muscle in a single session forces you to drop the weight as sets pile up and gives poor results
Spreading 9 sets as 3 sets on 3 days allows heavier weight, more tonnage, higher intensity and much better recovery
Recovery-tank analogy: 9 sets once a week drain you to zero and you recover from one stimulus, while 3 sets three times a week each drain about 30% and deliver roughly double the quality work
2-4 sets per muscle per session is the most conservative and productive range; every one of his programs uses it
Six sets per muscle in one session is impractical because the fatigue forces a lower frequency to recover
Only one set per muscle per session leaves volume on the table: too little tonnage and stimulus; too much and too little both end in no gains
His bodybuilding philosophy is to repeat the sets as often as possible: damage fibers, recover, rinse and repeat forever
48 hours of recovery pairs naturally with 2-4 sets per session; if you are forced to wait 72 hours between sessions for a muscle you can do more than 4 sets
Rough math: treat the week as about 8 days, halve it into about 4 sessions at 2-4 sets, giving about 7-14 sets per muscle per week, which matches the 8-15 that YouTube recommends
Lifters arrived at 2-4 sets, 48 hours between muscle groups and 7-14 weekly sets by instinct 30-40 years ago, before science backed it up
The hard answer for people who want a number: 8 to 14 sets per muscle per week
The optimal number of sets is whatever produces growth; it is a tautology, and you must decide for yourself
When guessing, err slightly high: too few sets means stagnation or regression, too many means at worst some junk volume or poorer recovery
Poor recovery is better than no recovery at all because there was no muscle damage to recover from, unless taken to the extreme
Be conservative when adding sets and liberal when removing them; trimming a set from a day is easy, adding risks too much volume at once
The optimal set number is an approximation; missing or adding one or two sets will not cost your gains
Overshooting sets is for experienced lifters; novices should get as much as possible from as few hard sets as possible with conservative weights and higher reps, as in his novice program
Add sets 1-2 per week and only when needed; if 3 weekly sets of squats are producing growth there is no reason to add more
Beginners and early intermediates doing 18-20 weekly sets have been brainwashed by bodybuilding channels; go back to hard sets with real weights and relevant rep ranges
If you do 4-6 or 4-8 sets per session, a 72-hour frequency is more suitable because it allows more time to recover
Rep range changes everything: 3x15 is not 3x3; nine sets of one is a waste of time, nine sets of ten in a day is idiotic junk volume
Extreme daily volume like 15 sets in a day might need around 100 hours of recovery, so you are better off doing less more often
Very low sets per session do not let you recover in 24 hours because tendon and nervous fatigue still accumulate; Bulgarian-style daily training for bodybuilding fails
Almost no one needs 16-20 weekly sets per muscle; focus on set quality instead
20 weekly sets would require 5 days x 4 sets or 2 days x 10 sets, and neither makes sense for recovery, showing the number is impractical
Frequency dictates templates, not the other way round: choose your preferred frequency first, then the split
48-hour frequency suits upper/lower, 72-hour suits push/pull/legs, 24-hour suits daily full body without killing yourself each session, and full body 3x/week gives 48 or 72 hours
Absolute training frequency is not muscle-group frequency: you can train 7 days a week yet hit biceps only once
Decide frequency before sets: if you train 3 days a week, set the per-muscle sets for each day from that
Most generic programs look artificial because they are built for no specific human; only you can tailor a program by choosing your own frequency
Evolving sets (a weekly range such as 8-12 sets instead of a fixed 12) are reserved for advanced lifters because swinging sets changes volume far more than swinging reps
A set range gives freedom on low-motivation weeks while still enforcing a minimum, and teaches that set numbers are not fixed
Programming is simple if you allow yourself to be wrong; the simple approach is as effective as the galaxy-brain calculation and is the one he recommends
